opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say our approach is to start from the technology and be honest about what it can and can't do yet, rather than starting from a slide deck about a big market.

A lot of teams in AI right now build a product first and then hope the model will catch up. We try to do it the other way around. We spend a lot of time understanding the core capability: where the model reasons well, where it breaks, and why it breaks. Once we have a clear picture, we ask which real problems that capability actually solves today, not two years from now.

On commercialization, we try to stay close to a small number of users who really care about the problem. Early on, it's much more valuable to have ten people who use the system every day and tell you exactly where it fails than a thousand people who try it once. Their feedback goes straight back into research, so the product and the research aren't separate tracks. They feed each other.

We're also careful not to over-promise. In this field it's very tempting to market a demo as if it were a finished system. But if users rely on something and it fails in a way they didn't expect, you lose their trust, and that's very hard to win back. We'd rather ship something narrower that works reliably and then expand the scope as the underlying technology gets stronger.

So in short: research-driven, close to users, and honest about the boundary between what's real and what's still a hope.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research-driven, user-focused approach to products and commercialization, but does not link that approach to team members’ prior experience starting companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we start from the technical problem rather than from a product spec. Most of my career has been on the research side, so our instinct is to ask what's actually hard and unsolved, work on that in the open, and let the applications reveal themselves once the capability exists. A lot of the things that ended up being useful commercially weren't planned as products at all.

That said, I don't think research and commercialization are in tension. The best feedback a research team can get comes from real workloads with real constraints: latency, cost, reliability, users who don't behave the way your benchmark assumes. When you put a model or a system in front of actual users, you find out very quickly which of your assumptions were wrong, and that pushes the research in directions you wouldn't have found by yourself. So we try to keep a tight loop: publish and open-source what we build, let people stress it, and bring those lessons back into the next round of fundamental work.

The other principle is that we don't chase every trend. There is enormous pressure right now to turn everything into a demo or a product launch, and that's a fast way to end up doing shallow work. We'd rather pick a few problems we believe matter over a multi-year horizon, go deep on them, and be comfortable that the commercial payoff may arrive later and in a form we didn't predict. If the foundation is solid, the products tend to follow.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research-led approach and feedback from real users, but does not link that approach to team members’ prior experience starting companies.

astra-6.text:
Our approach is to start with the research and understand what the technology can actually do, while staying close to practical problems. There’s often a gap between a promising research result and something people can reliably use. Closing that gap takes a lot of engineering, iteration, and feedback.

So we try to make it a two-way process: research creates new possibilities for products, and product experience reveals where the research still needs to improve. Commercialization depends on whether we can turn a capability into something that consistently solves a real problem for users.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research-led, iterative path to products and commercialization, but does not link that approach to team members’ prior experience starting companies.

sol-6.1.text:
We tend to start with the research: can we get something to work, and does it offer a meaningful improvement? But a research result isn’t automatically a product. You also have to understand who needs it, how it fits into their workflow, and whether it’s reliable and economical enough to use.

So I see commercialization as a feedback loop. You put an early version in front of users, learn where the real value is, and let that inform the next round of research. The key is keeping the research and product teams close enough that they can learn from each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research-to-product feedback loop, but does not link that approach to team members’ prior experience starting companies.
